2021 · ICML 2021 · Benchmarks & Evals

AGENT: A Benchmark for Core Psychological Reasoning

A procedurally generated, physics-rendered 3D video benchmark that borrows violation-of-expectation experiments from infant cognitive science to test whether machine agents share the pre-verbal intuitive psychology every human toddler already has.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By the time they can walk, human infants already possess a rich intuitive psychology: they distinguish agents from inert objects, expect agents to act efficiently toward their goals under whatever physical constraints apply, infer hidden obstacles from a detour they never directly observed, and read an agent's relative preferences off how much cost it is willing to pay to get something. None of this requires language or explicit instruction — it is the "core" psychological reasoning studied by decades of developmental-psychology violation-of-expectation experiments (Woodward, 1998; Gergely et al., 1995; Csibra et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2017).

Machine learning had, by 2021, produced several models that claim to reason about other agents' mental states — Bayesian inverse-planning models building on Baker et al. (2017), and neural Theory-of-Mind networks such as Rabinowitz et al.'s ToMnet (2018). But the authors argue there was no rigorous benchmark for asking whether these models actually acquire the same core concepts infants have, as opposed to fitting narrow, scenario-specific statistical patterns. Existing ToM evaluations mostly tested models on trials drawn from the same distribution they were trained on; they did not stress-test whether the "reasoning" survives a new physical configuration, a new obstacle type, or an entirely different psychological concept than the one seen in training. AGENT (Action, Goal, Efficiency, coNstraint, uTility) is built to close exactly that gap: a large, human-validated, procedurally generated dataset structured around four scenarios, paired with a generalization-first evaluation protocol, rather than a single train/test split from one distribution.

The paper is explicit about scope: AGENT does not test false belief or other richer facets of Theory of Mind — only the "core" psychological concepts (efficient action, hidden constraints, cost-reward trade-offs, goal preference) that are already present in children too young to pass false-belief tasks. A concurrent, independently developed benchmark, BIB (Baby Intuitions Benchmark; Gandhi et al., 2021), targets an overlapping but distinct set of concepts using maze-like 2D-ish environments; AGENT instead simulates diverse 3D physical situations (ramps, platforms, doors, bridges, chasms) and adds scenarios BIB does not cover (unobserved constraints, cost-reward trade-offs), while emphasizing cross-scenario and cross-type generalization rather than whether a concept can be learned from one big training set at all.

// how it works

The method

AGENT is not a text or QA benchmark: it is a video-based, violation-of-expectation task. Every trial is a short sequence of 3D animations rendered in the TDW (ThreeDWorld) physics-simulation engine, showing a simple agent (a sphere, cone, or cube) moving among goal objects and obstacles (walls, ramps, platforms, chasms, doors, bridges — see the object/obstacle catalogue below). Each trial has two phases: a familiarization phase (one or more videos of an agent's typical behavior — most scenarios show one, but Scenario 4's cost-reward trials show four) and a test phase, showing either a new physical situation or the same scene with a previously occluded region now revealed. Every test video is labeled expected (behavior consistent with what was seen in familiarization) or surprising (the agent goes for a different goal, moves inefficiently, or otherwise violates what the familiarization videos implied). A model's job is to output a "surprise rating" for a test video, and accuracy is measured over matched expected/surprising pairs that share the same familiarization video(s): the fraction of pairs where the model rates the surprising video as more surprising than its expected twin — the same relative-ranking metric used in Riochet et al.'s IntPhys (2018).

The four scenarios each isolate a different core-psychology concept, and each is further split into multiple trial "types" that vary the physical setup to rule out simple heuristics:

  • Scenario 1 — Goal Preferences (4 types, 1.1–1.4): the agent prefers one of two objects; does it keep pursuing the preferred object when the physical cost of reaching either object changes between familiarization and test?
  • Scenario 2 — Action Efficiency (5 types, 2.1–2.5): does the agent take the most efficient path given the obstacles actually present, rather than blindly repeating its familiarization path (e.g. when an obstacle is removed, made smaller, changed in kind, or moved out of the way)?
  • Scenario 3 — Unobserved Constraints (2 types, 3.1–3.2): after seeing an agent take a costly, curved detour partly hidden behind an occluder, does the model correctly expect the occluder to reveal an obstacle that justifies that detour?
  • Scenario 4 — Cost-Reward Trade-offs (2 types, 4.1–4.2): having watched the agent give up on a goal once the obstacle got hard enough, does the model infer the agent's relative preference and predict which of two goals it will choose under a new combination of obstacle costs?

The released dataset has 8,400 videos (5.6–25.2 s each, 35 fps) forming 3,360 trials — 1,920 training, 480 validation, and 960 test trials (480 matched expected/surprising pairs). Training and validation trials contain only expected videos; the surprising variant is reserved for the held-out test pairs, since neither baseline is trained as a classifier — both are trained to predict an agent's expected trajectory and then score surprise as the deviation between that prediction and what the test video actually shows.

Two baselines are compared, both given oracle ground-truth 3D state (bounding boxes and color codes for every agent/object/obstacle, as provided by the TDW simulator) rather than raw pixels in the paper's main results:

BIPaCK (Bayesian Inverse Planning and Core Knowledge) recreates the scene in a separate physics engine (PyBullet), representing obstacles as cubes and the agent/objects as spheres, and treats the agent's reward-per-goal-object R and cost-function weights w as latent parameters to be inferred. An RRT*-based planner samples trajectories that jointly maximize goal reward and minimize movement cost:

Γ̂ = arg maxΓ  Σg rg·δ(sTa, sg) − Σt C(sta, st+1a) // C(sₐ, s′ₐ) = wᵀf — cost is a weighted sum of the force needed to move the agent

The likelihood of an observed trajectory is exponential in its (dynamic-time-warped) distance to the model's best sampled trajectory; the posterior over physics/agent parameters is calibrated on the training trials, then updated per-trial using the familiarization video(s) before scoring the test video's surprise as the expected distance between predicted and observed trajectories.

ToMnet-G extends Rabinowitz et al.'s ToMnet with a graph neural network: every entity (agent, object, obstacle) becomes a graph node carrying its class, bounding box, and color; a GNN + LSTM encodes each familiarization video into a pooled "character" embedding, which is combined with a GNN+LSTM encoding of the test video's initial state to produce a "mental state" embedding that an MLP decodes into a per-step trajectory update (x̂t+1 ← x̂t + δx), trained end-to-end with an MSE trajectory-prediction loss. For Unobserved Constraints trials, both models first reconstruct the occluded portion of the trajectory (removing the occluder from the state and curve-fitting the missing segment) before scoring surprise.

// what they found

The results

The authors first validated the trials themselves with 300 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants, who rated 240 sampled test trials (25% of the test set, covering all trial types and obstacles) on a 0–100 surprise slider, each trial rated by 10 participants (about 8 trials per participant). Averaged across an ensemble of raters, the surprising video was rated more surprising than its expected pair 100% of the time; standardizing individual raters' scales and applying the same paired-ranking metric used for models gives an estimated single-human accuracy of 0.91 overall (Table 1's rightmost "All" column).

When trained and tested on all four scenarios together (the "All" condition, still using oracle 3D state), BIPaCK reaches 0.96 overall accuracy — above the 0.91 individual-human estimate — with near-ceiling scores in every scenario (Goal Preferences 0.99, Action Efficiency 0.97, Unobserved Constraints 0.90, Cost-Reward Trade-offs 0.95). ToMnet-G reaches 0.90 overall in this same in-distribution condition, close to BIPaCK, but its per-type profile is uneven: it hits 1.0 on several individual types (e.g. Goal Preferences Types 1.2 and 1.4) while dropping to 0.57 on Type 1.1 and 0.67 on Type 1.3 — a pattern the authors attribute to exploiting a low-level heuristic (in Types 1.2/1.4, the agent always moves away from the object requiring the higher-cost obstacle) rather than genuinely reasoning about costs and preferences.

The sharper split shows up under the two headline generalization tests. In G1 (leave-one-trial-type-out), BIPaCK's overall accuracy barely moves — 0.94 — while ToMnet-G collapses to 0.65, including a near-floor 0.05 on held-out Action Efficiency Type 2.5 (versus 1.0 on that same type when it was part of the training distribution) and 0.45 on Type 2.3. In G2 (leave-one-scenario-out) — training on three scenarios and testing cold on the fourth — BIPaCK again holds at 0.94 overall, while ToMnet-G reaches only 0.71, dropping to 0.35 on Action Efficiency Type 2.1, below the 0.5 chance level of the pairwise-ranking metric.

The paper also reports the correlation between each model's per-type accuracy and human per-type accuracy across all thirteen trial types: 0.55 for BIPaCK versus 0.06 for ToMnet-G — evidence that BIPaCK's easy/hard trials line up with humans' far more than ToMnet-G's do. Two additional generalization tests, G3 (train on one type, test on the rest of that scenario) and G4 (train on one scenario, test on the other three), tell the same story: BIPaCK is close to flat across held-out conditions, with its single largest failure being Action Efficiency Type 2.3 — when trained on Types 2.1, 2.2, or 2.4 individually and evaluated on held-out Type 2.3, its accuracy drops to 0.65, 0.70, and 0.75 respectively, a mis-estimated cost function causing it to predict the agent detours around a wall rather than jumping over it. ToMnet-G's G3/G4 failures are broader and land closer to or below chance on several off-diagonal cells (highlighted in the figure below).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

AGENT is a carefully constructed diagnostic — human-validated, procedurally generated so its "surprising" label is authored rather than subjective, and explicit about the narrow slice of Theory of Mind it targets. But the headline comparison it is best known for — a hand-engineered planner beating a learned network on generalization — needs several qualifiers before it supports the paper's broader framing that "a model must acquire or have built-in representations of how agents plan" to pass these tests.

baselines

The two baselines are not comparably resourced. BIPaCK bakes in a physics engine (PyBullet), an RRT* motion planner, and a Bayesian inverse-planning framework built directly on Baker et al.'s (2017) rational-agent model — it is handed the correct hypothesis space for "agents plan to maximize reward minus cost" by construction. ToMnet-G is a comparatively small GNN+LSTM trained from scratch on only 1,920 training trials, with no physics prior and no planning module. The result — a model with the right inductive bias beats a small, from-scratch neural net on out-of-distribution generalization — is a real and useful finding, but it is a finding about this specific architecture pairing on a small dataset, not a general verdict on whether any learned representation can achieve core psychological reasoning. No large video-pretrained model or world model was evaluated.

contamination

Not the usual web-scraping concern — AGENT is entirely synthetic, generated by a scene-graph sampler and rendered in TDW, so there is no pretraining-corpus leakage to worry about for the released videos themselves. The more relevant leakage-adjacent issue is informational: every trial's ground-truth label is generated by the same procedural rule that authors "expected" vs. "surprising," so the benchmark cannot surface disagreement about what should count as surprising — it only tests whether a model's ranking matches the generator's design intent, which is exactly what both baselines were built to match by inductive bias, not learned inference.

what's missed

All of Table 1's headline numbers use ground-truth 3D bounding boxes and color codes extracted directly from the TDW simulator — the paper states results from perception-model-extracted states are reported only in the supplementary material, which is not part of the 12-page arXiv main text. That means the benchmark's central claim about "core psychological reasoning" is validated in a setting where object detection, tracking, and identity persistence across occlusion are solved by fiat, not by the model. The accuracy metric is also a forced pairwise ranking (surprising rating > expected rating) rather than a calibrated score, so it can't distinguish a model with a large, confident surprise margin from one that barely edges ahead by chance; and human validation covered only 240 of the 960 test trials (25%), with no report of inter-rater agreement per trial type.

would raise confidence

Reporting the perception-based (non-oracle-state) numbers as a primary result rather than a supplementary appendix; adding a modern large-scale video or world model as a third baseline so "built-in physics beats a small GNN" can be checked against "a big pretrained video model beats a small GNN"; a no-familiarization ablation confirming that surprise ratings genuinely depend on the familiarization video rather than static per-frame cues; and calibration analysis (not just paired ranking) on the full 960-trial test set.

// bottom line

AGENT is a rigorous, well-validated instrument for exposing a real failure mode — a from-scratch neural Theory-of-Mind network (ToMnet-G) that looks strong in-distribution (0.90 overall) but collapses under held-out generalization (0.65–0.71, with individual cells at or below chance), while a model handed the right built-in physics-and-planning prior (BIPaCK) stays flat (0.94 in both generalization tests). That is a genuinely useful diagnostic result. It is not, on its own, evidence that learned representations in general cannot achieve core psychological reasoning — only that this particular from-scratch network, under oracle perception and a few-thousand-trial training budget, did not.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AGENT is a synthetic, TDW-rendered 3D video benchmark (8,400 videos, 3,360 two-phase familiarization→test trials) organized around four developmental-psychology scenarios — Goal Preferences, Action Efficiency, Unobserved Constraints, and Cost-Reward Trade-offs — scored by whether a model ranks a "surprising" test video above its matched "expected" twin.
  2. Given oracle 3D state, a hand-engineered Bayesian Inverse Planning + physics baseline (BIPaCK) scores 0.96 overall in-distribution and holds at 0.94 under both leave-one-type-out and leave-one-scenario-out generalization tests, versus an estimated individual-human accuracy of 0.91.
  3. A learned graph-network Theory-of-Mind baseline (ToMnet-G) scores a comparable 0.90 in-distribution but collapses to 0.65 and 0.71 under the same two generalization tests — including a 0.05 (near-floor) score on a held-out trial type it scored 1.0 on when in-distribution — the paper's central evidence that its architecture overfits to scenario-specific heuristics rather than learning the underlying psychological concept.
  4. Every headline number in the main paper assumes ground-truth object/agent state rather than raw perception, and results on extracted (non-oracle) states are relegated to a supplementary appendix — a real limit on how far "BIPaCK beats ToMnet-G" generalizes to an agent that has to perceive the scene itself.
